title: Build a barrel stove from a steel drum
summary: Turn a clean steel drum and a kit door, legs and flue collar into a wood heater for a shop, garage or cabin. The drum is the danger: one that held fuel or chemicals can explode when you cut it, and the thin, unlisted steel needs bigger clearances than a real stove and wears out.

materials.item: Steel drum with bungs, 208 L (55 US gal), not galvanised, that held only water or is made clean as the hot-work card says
Barrel stove kit: cast-iron door, legs, 150 mm (6 in) flue collar with damper, bolts (US Stove, Vogelzang or similar)
Double-barrel adapter legs and second flue collar
Dry sand, or firebrick or loose gravel, for the bottom
Black single-wall stovepipe, 150 mm (6 in), 24 gauge or heavier, with elbows
Insulated 650 °C chimney (ULC S629 or UL 103HT) with its thimble or ceiling support, supports and cap
Steel mesh for a spark arrester, 6 mm (¼ in) openings
Non-combustible floor: concrete or stone, or a pad built as the stove install guide sets for a non-listed stove
materials.qty: under the stove and at least 450 mm (18 in) beyond the door

materials.item: Sheet-steel heat shields, 29 gauge or thicker, held off the wall by at least 21 mm (7/8 in) on non-combustible spacers

steps.text: Decide where it goes. Barrel-stove kits are sold for shops, garages, cabins and camps, not for heating homes, and never for mobile homes (US Stove kit page, Cleveland kit manual, US Stove kit manual).
steps.warn: In a living space it is an uncertified stove with walls about 1 mm thick. Use it only if nothing better exists, with the biggest clearances, a proper chimney and alarms.

steps.text: Pick the drum: steel with bung plugs in one end, 208 L (55 US gal), not plastic, not galvanised, and thoroughly clean inside (US Stove kit manual, Cleveland kit manual). Best is one you know held only water; any other drum goes through the hot-work card first (NZ OSH drums).
steps.warn: Fuel, oil, solvent, paint or unknown contents: work through the hot-work card first, or choose another drum. Galvanised steel gives off zinc oxide fume when hot (CCOHS fumes), which causes metal fume fever (NIOSH zinc oxide).

steps.text: Outdoors, open both bungs, drain it and wash it out. Fill it to the brim with water to push out any vapour, then drain it again (Cleveland kit manual). Water only suits a drum that held water-soluble things: it does not wash out petrol, oil, grease or solvent (NZ OSH drums), so for those use the hot-work card first.
steps.warn: Never a torch on a drum (US Stove kit manual). A grinder spark lit vapour in a closed drum in an Ottawa high-school class in 2011 and killed a student (CHRR Ottawa).

steps.text: Stand the drum on end, bungs up. Mark round the inside of the door frame and the air inlet on the bung end, placing the door over the small bung (US Stove kit manual, Cleveland kit manual).
Cut the openings with a hacksaw or sabre saw, then file the edges smooth (US Stove kit manual, Cleveland kit manual).
steps.warn: Cut sheet steel is razor sharp: leather gloves and eye protection.

steps.text: Bed the door frame in high-temperature sealant and bolt it on. Seal any extra holes beside the bungs (Cleveland kit manual).
Lay the drum down. Reach in through the door to bolt on the legs near the front and back, so the drum sits level and steady (US Stove kit manual, Cleveland kit manual).
Mark and cut the hole for the 150 mm (6 in) flue collar on top at the back, bed the collar in sealant, bolt it on and fit the damper (Cleveland kit manual, US Stove kit manual).
Put about 5 cm (2 in) of dry sand in the bottom, or line it with firebrick or loose gravel, to protect the thin steel (US Stove kit manual, Cleveland kit manual).
Burn it off outdoors before it comes inside: a hot fire on bare ground, everyone upwind, until the paint and any lining stop smoking.
steps.warn: Burning coatings give off CO, hydrogen chloride or isocyanates, and old primer may hold lead (CCOHS fumes). Keep children away.

steps.text: Set it on a non-combustible floor or pad at least 1,200 mm (48 in) from walls that burn at the sides and back and 1,830 mm (72 in) at the front and above (NRCan wood heating, Cleveland kit manual).
steps.warn: Cleveland's label says not for use on combustible flooring (Cleveland kit manual), and NRCan says an uncertified stove's floor protection depends on its leg height and bottom protection (NRCan wood heating): see the stove install guide. Wall shields need an air gap on non-combustible spacers.

steps.text: Connect 150 mm (6 in) black single-wall pipe, crimped ends toward the stove, three screws a joint, to an insulated 650 °C chimney (NRCan wood heating), with a listed thimble where it passes through a combustible wall (Drolet Part 1); the pipe is 6 in (US Stove kit manual).
steps.warn: Single-wall pipe is a connector only: never through a combustible floor or ceiling, an attic, roof space, closet or hidden space (Drolet Part 1). Through a combustible wall only as CSA B365 sets (Drolet Part 1). No galvanised pipe (NRCan wood heating), no dryer duct.

steps.text: Fit a spark arrester of 6 mm (¼ in) steel mesh on the chimney top; no opening bigger than 1 cm (USFS sheepherder stove, SOPFEU spark arrestor).
steps.warn: Fine mesh plugs with soot and chokes the fire in under an hour (USFS sheepherder stove); a blocked chimney can send smoke into the room (NRCan wood heating). Brush it every time you check the chimney.

steps.text: Fit a smoke alarm and a CO alarm in the room, keep an ABC extinguisher close, and start with small fires. Never use petrol or other flammable liquid to light it (US Stove kit manual).
Inspect the pipe and chimney at least twice a month in the season (US Stove kit manual), and the drum weekly for thin spots, bulges and holes. Replace the drum when it rusts through.
steps.warn: Glowing steel means overfiring (US Stove kit manual). A hole in the drum leaks smoke and CO.

notes:
## What a barrel stove is, and what it isn't
A barrel stove is a steel drum laid on its side with a bolt-on door, legs and a flue collar. Kits sell the cast-iron parts: US Stove's BSK1000 has the door, legs, a 150 mm (6 in) flue collar with damper and the bolts, for a 36 or 55 US gal steel drum (US Stove kit page). US Stove's brands page lists Vogelzang (US Stove brands). Cleveland Iron Works, a Mr. Heater brand, sold a similar kit (Cleveland kit manual). Double-barrel adapters put a second drum on legs above the first, so the hot gases pass through it before the chimney (US Stove kit manual, Cleveland kit manual).

Read the makers' own limits before you plan on one for the house:
- US Stove: not EPA certified and **not intended for residential heating**; meant for workshops, cabins, garages and camping (US Stove kit page).
- Cleveland: install it only outside of any home, **not for indoor residential use**, never in a mobile home, and never on a combustible floor (Cleveland kit manual). US Stove's kit sheet also bars mobile homes (US Stove kit manual).
- In Canada, a stove from a small informal welding shop counts as uncertified: it needs larger clearances, burns dirtier, makes more creosote and may be a serious fire hazard (NRCan wood heating).

So: a shop, garage or outbuilding first. If a barrel stove is the only heat you have for a living space, treat it as an uncertified stove with thin walls, give it the biggest clearances below, and fit it to a proper chimney with alarms. A found certified stove is better: [Check and fix a found wood stove](#guides/repair_wood_stove).

## The drum
| Fact | Figure | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Capacity | 208 L (55 US gal) | Repackify drums |
| Size | 572 mm (22.5 in) across, about 851 mm (33.5 in) tall, closed-head | Repackify drums |
| Empty weight | about 17 to 22 kg (38 to 48 lb) | Repackify drums |
| Steel | about 1 mm; 16 to 22 gauge; Cary's example has a 0.9 mm body with 1.2 mm and 1.5 mm ends | Repackify drums, Cary drums |
| Codes | 1A1 = tight (closed) head with bungs; 1A2 = open head with a lid and ring | Cary drums |

Kits are made for steel drums with bung plugs in one end, and the door bolts on over the small bung (US Stove kit manual). Plastic drums are out (Cleveland kit manual). US Stove's sheet says 30 US gal minimum, Cleveland's 55 (US Stove kit manual, Cleveland kit manual).

**What it held decides everything.** A new drum, or one you know held only water, is the easy case. A drum that held fuel, oil, solvent, paint, cleaner or anything you can't name can explode when you cut it, even years after it was emptied, and labels can be wrong because drums get reused (NZ OSH drums, HSE drum bulletin). WorkSafe Victoria's rule is simple: if you don't know what a container held, don't put heat on it (WorkSafe Vic drums). Work through [Hot work on drums, tanks and cylinders](#guides/safety_hot_work_containers) first, or pick another drum.

**No galvanised drums.** Heated zinc gives off zinc oxide fume, which causes metal fume fever: chills, aches, nausea, fever, dry throat and cough (NIOSH zinc oxide, CCOHS fumes). In a Forest Service test, galvanised stovepipe on a tent stove passed 760 °C (1,400 °F) and the coating vaporised into toxic fumes (USFS sheepherder stove). A stove runs hot every day, so a galvanised body would fume every time. [Rocket stove](#guides/build_rocket_stove) shows how to spot zinc coating.

**Lined drums.** Some drums carry an inner epoxy-phenolic lining, and unlined ones a thin rust-inhibitor film (Cary drums). Expect lining and paint to smoke and burn on the first hot fire.

## Old tanks
- **Compressor air tanks** are steel, but the water drained from them carries oil and rust, and standing water rusts the wall thin from inside (CP condensate). Oils that don't catch fire when cold give off flammable vapour when heated (NZ OSH drums); an oil drum cut with a flame cutter exploded and the lid hurt the operator (HSE INDG314). Treat an air tank as a fuel container.
- **Propane cylinders** are the hardest case and the existing advice is not to cut them at all: see the hot-work card.

## Burning off paint and lining
Heated coatings give off toxic gases: epoxy gives carbon monoxide, vinyl paint hydrogen chloride, polyurethane isocyanates, and old primers may hold lead (CCOHS fumes). Do the first hot fire **outdoors**, before the drum comes inside: on bare ground away from anything that burns, everyone upwind, children and pets well away, until it stops smoking. Expect the outside to smoke too. Don't grind paint off: the dust may be toxic (CCOHS fumes).

## Clearances and floor
Kits give clearances from their own manuals; the Canadian code's figures for an uncertified radiant stove are bigger in places. Use the bigger number each way.

| Direction | US Stove kit | Cleveland kit | Uncertified stove, CSA B365 (via NRCan) | Use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sides and back, to walls that burn | 915 mm (36 in) | 915 mm (36 in) | 1,200 mm (48 in) | 1,200 mm (48 in) |
| Front (door end) | not given | 1,830 mm (72 in) | 1,200 mm (48 in) | 1,830 mm (72 in) |
| Above | not given | 1,830 mm (72 in) | 1,500 mm (60 in) | 1,830 mm (72 in) |
| Floor | not given | not on a combustible floor; 200 mm (8 in) legs | depends on leg height and bottom protection | non-combustible floor; over wood, only the set-ups in the install guide |

US Stove allows 100 mm (4 in) from a wall that is entirely non-combustible, such as concrete or masonry (US Stove kit manual). Cleveland's warning says the same, but its own table still lists 915 mm (36 in) to masonry (Cleveland kit manual), so give more when in doubt. A non-combustible covering over a wooden wall doesn't count (NRCan wood heating). Heat shields with an air gap cut the distances: see [Install a salvaged wood stove](#guides/build_stove_install) for the shield table, floor pad and pipe rules. Keep firewood, clothing, curtains and furniture well clear too: US Stove says the area round the heater must be kept free of anything that burns (US Stove kit manual).

## It wears out
The drum is about 1 mm of steel (Repackify drums), and neither kit maker gives it a service life. Cleveland says lining the bottom with firebrick or loose gravel protects the drum and lengthens its life; US Stove calls for about 5 cm (2 in) of sand (Cleveland kit manual, US Stove kit manual). In the Forest Service test, sand or dirt on the floor of a sheet-metal stove cut the heat reaching the ground beneath (USFS sheepherder stove). Even so, plan on replacing the drum: the kit parts unbolt and go onto a new one.

Look it over every week in the season, cold, with a light: flaking, thinning, bulges or pinholes, worst low down and round the door. A hole leaks smoke and carbon monoxide into the room. Glowing steel means you are overfiring it (US Stove kit manual): close the air and let it cool.

## Chimney and sparks
The kit must connect to a flue that goes outdoors (US Stove kit manual, Cleveland kit manual), and kits don't include the floor protector, connector pipe, thimble, shield or chimney (US Stove kit page). Single-wall pipe is a connector in the open room only; through a wall, ceiling or roof it takes insulated chimney in its own thimble ([Install a salvaged wood stove](#guides/build_stove_install)). Check the pipe and chimney for creosote at least twice a month in the heating season (US Stove kit manual).

**Spark arrester.** A mesh screen on the chimney top stops embers and keeps birds out; Quebec's forest-fire agency asks for openings no larger than 1 cm by 1 cm (SOPFEU spark arrestor). In the Forest Service tent-stove test, 6 mm (¼ in) mesh gave the best balance: 12 mm (½ in) let larger embers out, and 3 mm (⅛ in) plugged with soot and choked the stove in under an hour (USFS sheepherder stove). A plugged screen can push smoke and CO back into the room (NRCan wood heating names a blocked chimney as a cause of smoke in the house and of CO poisoning): brush it whenever you check the chimney.

## Living with it
- Fit a smoke alarm and a CO alarm in the room and keep an ABC extinguisher near ([Carbon monoxide](#guides/safety_carbon_monoxide)). Read the alarm's label for its temperature range: a cold shop or garage can sit below it before the stove warms the room (Kidde's alarms are made for 4 to 38 °C, 40 to 100 °F; Kidde temperature).
- Never start or freshen the fire with petrol or other flammable liquids. Ashes go in a metal container (US Stove kit manual), kept outdoors: ashes almost always hold live embers that stay hot for days and release carbon monoxide (Drolet Part 1), and live coals are a fire hazard (NRCan wood heating).
- The whole drum is a hot surface: keep it out of walkways and watch children closely (US Stove kit manual).
- Tend it rather than leave it: glowing steel means overfiring and children must not be left alone with it (US Stove kit manual), and a smouldering fire makes smoke, creosote and CO (NRCan wood heating). If it has to burn while people sleep, put the CO and smoke alarms where they will wake the sleepers and keep a way out clear ([Staying warm](#guides/skill_staying_warm)).
